newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-PRESS DIGEST-Australian Business News- Oct 14.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-PRESS DIGEST-Australian Business News- Oct 14.

text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

A survey conducted by The Australian Financial Review and the Australian Stock Exchange has found that some of Australia's largest companies paid almost no tax in 1995/96, with one of the lowest taxpayers, Lend Lease Corp, paying only 3.3 cents in every dollar of normal earnings. Page 1.

The Seven Network has launched legal action against Optus Vision that would see control of the pay-TV and telephony company go to Seven and would hamper the A$4 billion sharemarket listing of Optus Communications and the impending A$1 billion capital raising by its 46.5 percent-owned Optus Vision. Page 1.

According to the September quarter National Australia Bank survey of about 750 firms, profits and trading conditions both fell short of expectations in the latest three months and the manufacturing, wholesaling, retailing and property sectors were finding conditions most difficult. Page 3.

National Foods Ltd managing director Max Ould has given himself until Christmas to come up with a strategic plan for the company. Ould replaced Graham Reaney as manager of the fruit juice and packaging group in September and he acknowledges the market expects improvements at National Foods. Page 19.

Woolworths Ltd group managing director Reg Clairs remains optimistic about the Christmas trading period, despite seeing the group's target of double-digit sales growth slip away in the first three months of the year. Woolworths posted an 8.24 percent sales increase to A$3.85 billion for the three months to September. Page 19.

Following Australian Securities Commission investigations into abnormal trading in the lead-up to the A$2 billion TNT Ltd takeover bid by Dutch group KPN, TNT Ltd's auditor KPMG has moved to distance itself from the trading. Page 21.
THE AUSTRALIAN

Federal Resources Minister Warwick Parer believes Japan and Korea are becoming increasingly concerned about secure supply lines for imported energy resources, but they are still looking to Australia for reliable supplies of coal, uranium and natural gas to cater for the booming energy demands of future economic growth. Page 17.

It is understood a current assessment indicates a three million tonne, A$1 billion alumina refinery in the Malaysian State of Sarawak could be a financially stronger proposition for Comalco Ltd than a similar Queensland-based project, following the breakdwn of negotiations with the Queensland government over a guaranteed price paid by the state for excess electricity. Page 17.

Australian Bureau of Statistics figures reveal Australia's clothing and footwear production has taken a dive this year, as imported apparel goods flood the market and consumers spend their money on entertainment rather than shopping. The fashion sector's domestic output has dropped 18 percent in volume over the past year, as imports grew by 12 percent. Page 19.

The Electricity Supply Association of Australia has warned that misleading information on Australia's electricity prices is affecting the local industry's ability to compete and is inhibiting foreign investment. The association has launched a campaign to demostrate that domestic electricity prices in Australia are among the lowest in the world. Page 19.

A National Australia Bank survey of 750 companies has found that business conditions continued to worsen in the three months to September 1996, with a fall in orders, low profitability and the first fall in employment levels in three years. The survey suggested there could be room for another interest rate cut, possibly as soon as next month. Page 19.

As part of its move to demutualise and list on the Australian Stock Exchange early next year, Colonial Mutual is offering policyholders free shares worth at least A$580, but many are in danger of jeopardising the offer as Colonial will only mail out offer of shares and options when it is satisfied it has the correct address details, which many members have failed to confirm. Page 19.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

Australian National Industries director Peter Joseph is considering legal action over full page newspaper advertisements published on the weekend by fellow director Ross Palmer that called on shareholders to re-elect deputy chairman Fred Smith and Howard Stack as directors and to remove John Studdy and Joseph at the company's annual general meeting next week. Page 35.

Hoyts Cinemas managing director and major shareholder Peter Ivany has a grand plan to take Hoyts to all corners of the globe, and given the company's performance since its listing on the stock exchange in August - shares have risen from A$2 to A$2.82 - ivnestors have good reason to believe he will succeed. Page 35.

Colonial Group members will this week receive details of the life group's A$550 million public float ahead of a vote by members and policyholders on demutualisation and listing next month. It is expected the A$1.3 billion demutualisation wil go ahead following the successful A$2.7 billion float of rival insurance group National Mutual. Page 35.

The National Australia Bank's September quarter survey of 750 small, medium and large firms in all sectors of the economy has recorded the first drop in employment for three years, and its second consecutive contraction in trading conditions, confirming fears over the state of the economy. Page 35.

The directors of the Reef Casino Trust have said in a statement that the Cairns casino has suffered a shock A$5.9 million loss in the September quarter because of a significant shortfall in rental revenues and abnormal gaming losses. The trust missed outon its budgeted profit of A$900,000 and had breached the interest cover covenant required under its finance facility. Page 37.

Queensland Opposition finance spokesman David Hamill predicted yesterday that the Queensland Government will make a last minute A$1 billion bid to buy the Brisbane Airport. Hamill believes millions of dollars will be borrowed to buy the airport, which wil be launched later as a public company, offering shares to the public. Page 39.
THE AGE

Accounting firm Price Waterhouse has recruited a team of computer hackers to its forensic accounting unit in an attempt to infiltrate Australia's underworld of computer crime. The team of four will concentrate on the firewall security between internal sytems and internet sites. Page C1.

Financial high-flyer Rene Rivkin is set to shake up the insurance industry with the release of insurance products up to 30 percent below premiums offered by his mainstream rivals. His products would cover term life, trauma cover and income protection isurance under the title Rivkin Direct, an offshoot of the controversial Rivkin Croll Smith Insurance Agencies, launched in May. Page C1.

Ian Horton of Prudential Fund Managers and Sydney Futures Exchange head Les Hosking have criticised the Australian Stock Exchange's plan to abandon its mutual status and float as a public company. Horton said that because many of the ASX's function were not for profit he would not want to see them "minimised". Hosking said the futures exchange would watch the ASX very closely if it were to list, given their common interest in the share price index futures contract. Page C2.

The Yellow Pages Small Business Index, released last week, revealed that 52 percent of business owners would spend more time working on their businesses if freed from government regulatory obligations and paperwork and just over a quarter believed their profitability would significantly increase if they could spend less time complying with tax and regulatory obligations. Page C3.

When Carolyn and Kevin O'Brien planted a grove of cherry trees on their property at Mandurang in Victoria they did not realise the trees would blossom into an award-wining export business, Cherry Berry Fine Foods Group. Cherry Berry is now exporting goos worth A$1 million on exclusive supply contracts to airlines including Philippine Airlines and Ansett. Page C3.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 373-1800
